question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The event, in a cramped space, was totally bizarre in my view.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Odd.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Bizarre" means very strange, unusual, or eccentric; markedly different from the usual. (अजीब/विचित्र)
◦ Example: The tourists were amazed by the bizarre rock formations in the desert.

• In the given sentence, "The event, in a cramped space, was totally bizarre in my view", the word "bizarre" describes the event as strange/unusual, which is best matched by "Odd".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Usual" (सामान्य): Means normal or habitual — this is actually opposite in meaning to "bizarre", not a synonym.

• Option 2: "Customary" (प्रथागत): Means according to custom or usual practice — again nearly opposite to "bizarre".

• Option 4: "Normal" (सामान्य): Means conforming to a standard; ordinary — this too is an antonym, not a synonym, of "bizarre".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Bizarre": eccentric, weird, peculiar, outlandish, curious, freakish.

• Do not confuse "bizarre" (strange) with "bazaar" (a market) — the two are homophones often tested together in SSC vocabulary questions.

question: Select the sentence that has the correct use of spellings from the given options.
option_1: While the negociation process was complex and at times contentious, the two sides ultimately reached a mutually benificial aggreement.
option_2: While the negotiation process was complex and at times contentious, the two sides ultimately reached a mutually beneficial agreement.
option_3: While the nagotiation process was complex and at times contencious, the two sides ultimately reached a mutually beneficial agreement.
option_4: While the negotiation process was complex and at times contencious, the two sides ultimately reached a mutually beneficial aggreement.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. While the negotiation process was complex and at times contentious, the two sides ultimately reached a mutually beneficial agreement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 2 uses all four key words with their correct spellings: "negotiation", "contentious", "beneficial", and "agreement".

• Spelling rules to remember:
◦ Negotiation — from "negotiate"; note the sequence "go-ti-a-tion", not "go-ci-a-tion".
◦ Contentious — ends in "-tious", not "-cious" or "-cous".
◦ Beneficial — ends in "-ficial", not "-fical" or "-ficail".
◦ Agreement — has a double "e" ("agree" + "ment"); it is never written with a double "g" ("aggreement").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect: it misspells "negotiation" as "negociation" and "beneficial" as "benificial", and "agreement" as "aggreement".

• Option 3 is incorrect: it misspells "negotiation" as "nagotiation" and "contentious" as "contencious".

• Option 4 is incorrect: it misspells "contentious" as "contencious" and "agreement" as "aggreement".

NOTE

• Commonly misspelt words asked in SSC exams: accommodate, embarrass, questionnaire, occurrence, definitely, liaison, rhythm, and separate.

• A useful trick for "-tious" vs "-cious" endings: words derived from nouns ending in "-tion" (e.g. caution → cautious, ambition → ambitious) usually take "-tious"/"-cious" based on their root; when in doubt, memorise commonly tested words individually.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Frugality
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Extravagance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Frugality" means the quality of being economical with money or resources; thriftiness. (मितव्ययिता/किफायत)
◦ Example: His frugality allowed him to save a large part of his modest salary.

• The antonym of "Frugality" is "Extravagance", which means the habit of spending more money or resources than necessary; wastefulness. (फिजूलखर्ची)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Parsimony" (कंजूसी): Means extreme unwillingness to spend money — this is actually a near-synonym of "frugality", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Providence" (दूरदर्शिता/मितव्ययिता): Means foresight or thrifty provision for the future — again close in meaning to frugality, not opposite.

• Option 4: "Economy" (किफायत): Means careful management of resources — a synonym of frugality, not an antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Frugality": thrift, economy, prudence, austerity.

• Other synonyms of "Extravagance": lavishness, wastefulness, prodigality, squandering.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Moti has thrown the balls.
option_1: The balls were thrown by Moti.
option_2: The balls have been thrown by Moti.
option_3: The balls were being thrown by Moti.
option_4: The balls had been thrown by Moti.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The balls have been thrown by Moti.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Moti has thrown the balls" is in the Present Perfect Tense (Subject + has/have + V3 + Object).

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the balls" becomes the subject; since "balls" is plural, the auxiliary is "have"; and "thrown" (V3 of throw) is retained after "been".
◦ Passive: The balls have been thrown by Moti.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "were thrown" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, not the Present Perfect Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "were being thrown" is the passive form of the Past Continuous Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "had been thrown" is the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• The Present Perfect passive always uses the structure has/have + been + V3; do not confuse it with the Past Perfect passive, which uses had + been + V3.

• "Has" is used with singular subjects (he/she/it), and "have" is used with plural subjects and I/we/you/they.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.
Since the storm knocked in the power, we’ve been using candles to light our home.
option_2: the storm knocked out the power
option_3: the storm knocked over the power
option_4: the storm knocked away the power
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. the storm knocked out the power.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "the storm knocked in the power" uses the wrong preposition/particle with the phrasal verb "knock".

• The correct phrasal verb here is "knock out", which means to cause something (like electricity or a system) to stop working; to disable.
◦ Example: The heavy snowfall knocked out the power supply to the entire town.

• Since the sentence talks about losing electricity ("we've been using candles to light our home"), the intended meaning is that the storm disabled/cut off the power, which is correctly expressed by "knocked out the power".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No substitution required" is incorrect because "knocked in" is not an idiomatic or grammatically standard collocation with "power" in this context.

• Option 3: "the storm knocked over the power" is incorrect because "knock over" means to physically topple or overturn an object, which does not fit "power" (an abstract/electrical supply).

• Option 4: "the storm knocked away the power" is incorrect because "knock away" is not a standard idiomatic phrasal verb used with "power" in this sense.

NOTE

• Other common phrasal verbs with "knock": knock down (demolish/reduce price), knock off (stop work/deduct), knock up (prepare quickly, informal British usage), knock out (defeat/disable).

• "Power outage" and "power cut" are common collocations related to "knock out the power".

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the given situation.
Geetika spoke a lot about her new movie. However, it came to nothing in the theatres.
option_1: To give the devil his dues
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To end in smoke.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To end in smoke" means to come to nothing; to fail to produce any result despite effort or promise. (व्यर्थ जाना/धरा का धरा रह जाना)
◦ Example: All his grand plans for the business ended in smoke when the funding fell through.

• In the given situation, Geetika spoke a lot about her new movie, but it came to nothing in the theatres — exactly matching the meaning of "to end in smoke".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To give the devil his dues (निष्पक्ष होकर बुराई में भी अच्छाई देखना): To acknowledge the good qualities of a person one generally dislikes or disapproves of.

• Option 2: To get into hot water (मुसीबत में पड़ना): To get into trouble or a difficult situation.

• Option 3: To dig the grave (अपने पैरों पर कुल्हाड़ी मारना): To do something that will surely lead to one's own downfall or ruin (usually "dig one's own grave").

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "to fail/come to nothing": "to go up in smoke", "to fall through", "to come to naught", "to fizzle out".

• Do not confuse "end in smoke" with "there is no smoke without fire" (every rumour has some basis in truth).

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the underlined segment in the following sentence.
Raima takes her classes very attentively.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Be all ears.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Be all ears" means to listen with complete attention and eagerness. (पूरी तरह ध्यान से सुनना)
◦ Example: Go ahead and tell me the story — I'm all ears.

• In the given sentence, "Raima takes her classes very attentively", the underlined phrase "very attentively" is best replaced by the idiom "be all ears", which conveys the same sense of full, close attention.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: In accordance with (के अनुसार): Means in agreement with a rule or system; unrelated to attentiveness.

• Option 2: By blazing a trail (नया मार्ग प्रशस्त करना): Means to be the first to do something innovative; unrelated to attentiveness.

• Option 3: By losing in a cloud: Not a recognised standard English idiom, and does not relate to attentiveness (it appears to be a distractor confused with "to be on cloud nine" or "have one's head in the clouds").

NOTE

• Other idioms related to listening/attention: "to lend an ear" (to listen sympathetically), "to turn a deaf ear" (to ignore/refuse to listen), "to be all eyes" (to watch very attentively).

• "All ears" is always used predicatively, typically as "I'm all ears" or "be all ears", not as a standalone adverb.

question: Select the sentence that has the correct use of spellings from the given options.
option_1: Althogh the book was difficult to read, I persisted and eventualy understood the complex ideas.
option_2: Although the book was difficult to read, I persisted and eventually understood the complex ideas.
option_3: Although the book was difficult to read, I persisted and eventualy understood the complex ideas.
option_4: Although the book was difficult to read, I persested and eventually understood the complex ideas.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Although the book was difficult to read, I persisted and eventually understood the complex ideas.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 2 correctly spells all the key words: "Although", "persisted", and "eventually".

• Spelling rules to remember:
◦ Although — has the sequence "l-t-h", never "lthogh" or "lthough" without the correct letters.
◦ Eventually — is "event" + "ual" + "ly"; note the double "l" only at the very end ("-ually"), never "eventualy" or "eventualy".
◦ Persisted — from "persist"; the correct spelling has "sist", not "sest" ("persested" is wrong).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect: it misspells "Although" as "Althogh" and "eventually" as "eventualy".

• Option 3 is incorrect: it misspells "eventually" as "eventualy" (missing one "l").

• Option 4 is incorrect: it misspells "persisted" as "persested".

NOTE

• Commonly confused spellings: eventually vs. eventualy (wrong), definitely vs. definately (wrong), persistent vs. persistant (wrong).

• "Although" and "Though" are near-synonyms used to introduce a subordinate clause of contrast; both are frequently tested for spelling in SSC exams.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word given in brackets to fill in the blank.
The (friendly) dog wagged its tail, while the _____ cat hissed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. hostile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word given in brackets is "friendly", which means kind and pleasant; showing warmth. (मित्रतापूर्ण)

• The blank requires the antonym of "friendly" to contrast the dog's behaviour (wagging its tail) with the cat's behaviour (hissing).

• "Hostile" means unfriendly and aggressive; showing opposition or ill will, which is the exact opposite of "friendly" and fits the contrast with "hissed". (शत्रुतापूर्ण)
◦ Example: The dog greeted the visitor warmly, but the hostile cat hissed and ran away.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Loving" (प्रेमपूर्ण): A near-synonym of "friendly", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Welcoming" (स्वागत करने वाला): Also a near-synonym of "friendly", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Affectionate" (स्नेही): Also close in meaning to "friendly", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other antonyms of "friendly": unfriendly, aggressive, antagonistic, unwelcoming.

• Words like "hostile", "hissed", and "unfriendly" are commonly paired in SSC antonym-in-context questions to test whether the reader has understood the contrast implied by "while" in the sentence.

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in passive voice.
His brother needed some urgent help at that moment.
option_1: Some urgent help was needed by his brother at that moment.
option_2: Urgent help was needed by his brother at that moment.
option_3: Some urgent help is needed by his brother at that moment.
option_4: Some urgent help was needed by his brother at this moment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Some urgent help was needed by his brother at that moment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "His brother needed some urgent help at that moment" is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "some urgent help" (uncountable, singular) becomes the subject, so the auxiliary is "was"; the verb "needed" becomes "needed" (V3, same as V2 for regular verbs); "his brother" becomes the agent with "by"; and the adverbial "at that moment" must be retained unchanged.
◦ Passive: Some urgent help was needed by his brother at that moment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because it drops the word "some" from the object, changing the exact wording of the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is needed" is in the Simple Present Tense, whereas the original sentence is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it changes "that moment" to "this moment", altering the meaning/reference of the original sentence.

NOTE

• While converting active to passive voice, every word that is not part of the subject-verb-object structure (such as time/place adverbials — "at that moment", "yesterday", "in the garden") must be carried over into the passive sentence exactly as it appears in the active sentence.

• Determiners like "some", "a", "the" attached to the object must also be retained in the passive subject.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
Could you please tell me which languages you are fluent in?
option_1: you may be fluent in speaking
option_4: you have been fluent in speaking
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. you speak fluently.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined portion "you are fluent in" uses the adjective "fluent" with the preposition "in" (be + fluent + in + language).

• This can be correctly and concisely restated using the adverb "fluently" with the verb "speak": "you speak fluently", which conveys the identical meaning — the ability to speak a language with ease — in natural, grammatically correct English.
◦ Example: Tell me which languages you speak fluently.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "you may be fluent in speaking" is incorrect because it unnecessarily introduces the modal "may", which changes the meaning to possibility rather than a direct question about ability.

• Option 3: "you fluently speaking" is incorrect because it is not a grammatically complete verb phrase — it lacks an auxiliary verb (e.g., "are") before the present participle.

• Option 4: "you have been fluent in speaking" is incorrect because the Present Perfect-like structure changes the tense and meaning unnecessarily, and "fluent in speaking" is an awkward, non-idiomatic construction.

NOTE

• "Fluent" is an adjective and takes the preposition "in" (fluent in French); "fluently" is the corresponding adverb and is used directly with a verb (speaks fluently).

• Such substitution questions test the ability to convert an adjective + preposition construction into a natural verb + adverb construction without changing the meaning.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who lives a secluded or solitary life, often for religious reasons
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Monk.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Monk" means a person who lives a secluded or solitary life, often for religious reasons, typically as a member of a religious community bound by vows. (साधु/भिक्षु/मठवासी)
◦ Example: The monk spent most of his day in silent meditation inside the monastery.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Extrovert" (बहिर्मुखी व्यक्ति): A person who is energised by social interaction and enjoys being with others — nearly the opposite of the given definition.

• Option 2: "Chauvinist" (कट्टर पक्षपाती): A person with an excessive or biased belief in the superiority of their own group/cause; unrelated to a secluded religious life.

• Option 4: "Hypochondriac" (रोगभ्रम से ग्रस्त व्यक्ति): A person who is excessively anxious about their own health; unrelated to a secluded religious life.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Hermit/Recluse — a person who lives in solitude, avoiding society, not necessarily for religious reasons; Ascetic — a person who practises strict self-denial for religious reasons; Nun — a female member of a religious community living under vows.

• One-word substitution questions frequently test words describing lifestyles, professions, and personality types — building a list of such words (hermit, misanthrope, philanthropist, ascetic, nomad) is useful exam preparation.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Acclimatise
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Disarrange.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Acclimatise" means to make or become accustomed to a new climate, environment, or set of conditions; to settle or adjust in an orderly way. (नए वातावरण के अनुकूल होना)
◦ Example: It took the climbers a few days to acclimatise to the high altitude.

• Since "acclimatise" carries the sense of settling into order and adjustment, its listed opposite is "Disarrange", meaning to disturb the order of; to throw into disorder or confusion. (अस्तव्यस्त करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Prioritise" (प्राथमिकता देना): Means to arrange in order of importance — unrelated in meaning to "acclimatise".

• Option 3: "Placate" (शांत करना): Means to soothe or pacify someone's anger — unrelated in meaning to "acclimatise".

• Option 4: "Decriminalise" (अपराध की श्रेणी से हटाना): Means to remove legal restrictions on an act, making it no longer a criminal offence — unrelated in meaning to "acclimatise".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Acclimatise": adapt, adjust, accustom, familiarise, habituate.

• Other antonyms of "acclimatise" commonly listed: disturb, unsettle, confuse.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A) have to deal with
B) about the terrible traffic
C) on his way to work
D) Nishit begins thinking
E) he will surely
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. D, B, E, A, C.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Arranging the parts in the order D, B, E, A, C gives the meaningful sentence: "Nishit begins thinking about the terrible traffic he will surely have to deal with on his way to work."

• Rule — arranging jumbled sentence parts:
◦ Identify the subject and main verb first — here, "D) Nishit begins thinking" is the natural starting clause, since it introduces the subject and main verb.
◦ The object of thought must follow logically — "B) about the terrible traffic" naturally follows "thinking about".
◦ The remaining clause modifies "the terrible traffic" using a relative structure — "E) he will surely" + "A) have to deal with" together form a relative clause ("...traffic he will surely have to deal with"), and finally "C) on his way to work" completes the sentence by specifying when/where this happens.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (A, D, B, C, E) is incorrect because it starts with "have to deal with", which cannot logically be the beginning of the sentence.

• Option 2 (C, D, B, A, E) is incorrect because it starts with "on his way to work", separating the subject "Nishit" from the beginning of the sentence in an illogical way.

• Option 4 (E, B, A, D, C) is incorrect because it starts with "he will surely", but the pronoun "he" cannot be used before the noun "Nishit" is introduced.

NOTE

• In parajumbles/sentence-rearrangement questions, always locate the segment containing the main subject and verb first, and check that pronouns (he, she, it) never appear before the noun they refer to.

• Reading the fully reconstructed sentence aloud is the best final check for logical and grammatical coherence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
When I reached the market place, the coconuts was already sold.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. were already sold.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "When I reached the market place, the coconuts was already sold" contains a subject-verb agreement error: the subject "coconuts" is plural, but the verb "was" is singular.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A plural subject must take a plural verb. Since "coconuts" is plural, the correct auxiliary verb is "were", not "was" or "is".

• Also, since the main clause "When I reached the market place" is in the Simple Past Tense, the verb in the second clause must also be in the past tense: "were already sold".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "are already sold" is incorrect because "are" is present tense, which does not match the past tense of "reached".

• Option 2: "have already sell" is incorrect because it wrongly mixes the present perfect auxiliary "have" with the base form "sell" instead of the past participle "sold"; it is also present-tense, not matching "reached".

• Option 3: "is already sold" is incorrect because "is" is a singular auxiliary, which does not agree with the plural subject "coconuts", and it is also present tense.

NOTE

• Plural nouns (coconuts, books, cars) always take plural verb forms: are/were, not is/was.

• When the main clause of a sentence is in the past tense (e.g., "When I reached..."), the other clause(s) in the sentence must generally also be in a past tense form to maintain tense consistency.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
Gandhi’s approach, while effective in mobilising large segments of Indian society, was criticised by some for being passive and overly accommodating.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Disobliging.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "accommodating" means willing to fulfil others' wishes; helpful, cooperative, and easy to work with. (सहयोगी/समायोजनशील)
◦ Example: The accommodating landlord agreed to postpone the rent by a week.

• The antonym of "accommodating" is "Disobliging", meaning unwilling to help others; unhelpful and uncooperative. (असहयोगी)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Reconciling" (मेल कराने वाला): Means bringing about agreement or harmony — close to "accommodating" in spirit, not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Strenuous" (कठोर/श्रमसाध्य): Means requiring great effort or exertion — unrelated in meaning to "accommodating".

• Option 4: "Gratifying" (संतोषजनक): Means giving pleasure or satisfaction — unrelated in meaning, and not an opposite, of "accommodating".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "accommodating": obliging, helpful, cooperative, considerate.

• Other antonyms of "accommodating": unhelpful, uncooperative, inflexible, unyielding.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Tranquil
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Peaceful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Tranquil" means calm and peaceful; free from disturbance. (शांत)
◦ Example: The lake was tranquil in the early morning light.

• The closest synonym among the given options is "Peaceful", which also means calm and free from disturbance.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Anxious" (चिंतित): Means worried or uneasy — nearly opposite in meaning to "tranquil".

• Option 2: "Dilemma" (दुविधा): A noun meaning a situation requiring a difficult choice — not even the same part of speech as "tranquil" (an adjective), and unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: "Fierce" (उग्र): Means violent or aggressive — nearly opposite in meaning to "tranquil".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Tranquil": calm, serene, placid, still, undisturbed.

• Antonyms of "Tranquil": turbulent, chaotic, agitated, stormy.

question:
Select the grammatically correct version of the following sentence.
The young pirate is more cleverer than the captain of the ship.
option_1: The young pirate is cleverer to the captain of the ship.
option_2: The young pirate is cleverer than the captain of the ship.
option_3: The young pirate is most clever than the captain of the ship.
option_4: The younger pirate is cleverer than the captain of the ship.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The young pirate is cleverer than the captain of the ship.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The young pirate is more cleverer than the captain of the ship" contains a double comparative error: "more" and the comparative suffix "-er" (in "cleverer") are both used together, which is grammatically incorrect.

• Rule — Degrees of Comparison: For most two-syllable and all one-syllable adjectives, the comparative degree is formed by adding "-er" (e.g., clever → cleverer) OR by using "more" before the adjective (more clever) — never both together.

• Removing the redundant "more" gives the grammatically correct sentence: "The young pirate is cleverer than the captain of the ship."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it uses "cleverer to" instead of the correct comparative structure "cleverer than".

• Option 3 is incorrect because it uses "most clever" (the superlative degree, used to compare more than two items) to compare only two entities (the pirate and the captain), and comparisons between exactly two things must use the comparative degree ("more clever"/"cleverer than"), not the superlative.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it changes "young" to "younger", which alters the meaning of the original sentence unnecessarily (the original only compares cleverness, not age).

NOTE

• Comparative degree compares two things ("-er"/"more" + than); superlative degree compares three or more things ("-est"/"most" + the).

• Common double comparative errors to avoid: "more better", "most best", "more taller" — never combine "more/most" with an "-er/-est" form.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.
In course by time, / he was wise enough to realise / the mistakes of his past life.
option_2: he was wise enough to realise
option_3: the mistakes of his past life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. In course by time,

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct idiomatic phrase is "In course of time", meaning eventually; as time passes. The sentence incorrectly uses the preposition "by" instead of "of".

• Rule: Certain phrases in English are fixed idiomatic expressions in which the preposition cannot be substituted; "in course of time" is one such fixed phrase, and using any other preposition (like "by") makes it grammatically and idiomatically incorrect.

• The error therefore lies in the first part of the sentence: "In course by time,", which should read "In course of time,".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "he was wise enough to realise" is grammatically correct — "wise enough to + verb" is a standard, correctly used construction.

• Option 3: "the mistakes of his past life." is grammatically correct — the possessive structure and phrasing are accurate.

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist, in the first part of the sentence, as explained above.

NOTE

• Other fixed prepositional phrases frequently tested in SSC error-spotting: "in time" (early enough), "on time" (punctually), "in the course of" (during), "by and by" (gradually).

• Always check fixed idiomatic phrases carefully in error-spotting questions, since a single wrong preposition can make an otherwise well-formed sentence incorrect.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
The study of coins
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Numismatics.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Numismatics" means the study or collection of coins, paper currency, and medals. (सिक्का-विज्ञान/मुद्रा अध्ययन)
◦ Example: As a hobby, he took a keen interest in numismatics and collected coins from over fifty countries.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Currency" (मुद्रा): Refers to the system of money in general use in a country — it is the object being studied, not the name of the study itself.

• Option 2: "Minting" (सिक्का ढालना): Refers to the process of manufacturing coins, not the study of coins.

• Option 4: "Barter" (वस्तु-विनिमय): Refers to a system of exchanging goods/services without using money — unrelated to the study of coins.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Philately — the study or collection of postage stamps; Numismatist — a person who studies or collects coins.

• Such "-ics"/"-y" suffixed words naming fields of study (numismatics, philately, etymology, epistemology) are frequently tested in SSC one-word substitution questions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Daniel talks to people about the right to life. He says, “We have the right to live in freedom and in safety!” but the people do not (1)________ and they say that the War is a big deal and it is not up to us nor up to the government. The government knows what to do and only the government can decide (2)______ is best. And if the government says that there must be war, then it must be so. Daniel does not accept this and asks if there is a better solution. As all wars end with agreements, can’t we do the agreements without the fighting? Can’t the government solve this (3)_________? Isn’t that the reason we have a government in the first place? He decides to (4)______ to people in his government. He decides to write them and let them know what he thinks. He knows one opinion does not matter much, but he also knows that if everyone in his own country and on the other side would do this, there will (5)_________ be no more wars.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. agree.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"...but the people do not (1)________ and they say that the War is a big deal..." The word "but"** signals a contrast with Daniel's statement that people have the right to live in freedom and safety.

• Since the people go on to argue that the decision is not up to them ("it is not up to us nor up to the government"), they are clearly expressing disagreement with Daniel's view. The word that best fits the blank is therefore "agree" — "the people do not agree".

• Rule: In cloze passages, the word chosen must be grammatically correct in the sentence AND must logically fit the meaning/tone established by the surrounding context (here, the contrast introduced by "but").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "grant" does not fit — "grant" means to give or allow something formally, which does not make sense with "the people do not grant" in this context (grant what?).

• Option 3: "consent" is close in meaning but is typically followed by "to" (consent to something) and is a more formal/legalistic term; "agree" flows more naturally with the informal tone of the passage and directly signals disagreement with an opinion, which is what is being expressed here.

• Option 4: "announce" does not fit — "announce" means to make a public declaration, which does not match the sense of disagreeing with an idea.

NOTE

• Cloze passage questions require reading the whole passage (not just the sentence with the blank) to understand the tone and logical flow before choosing an option.

• "Agree" is followed by "with" (agree with a person/idea) or "to" (agree to a proposal); "consent" is followed by "to".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Daniel talks to people about the right to life. He says, “We have the right to live in freedom and in safety!” but the people do not (1)________ and they say that the War is a big deal and it is not up to us nor up to the government. The government knows what to do and only the government can decide (2)______ is best. And if the government says that there must be war, then it must be so. Daniel does not accept this and asks if there is a better solution. As all wars end with agreements, can’t we do the agreements without the fighting? Can’t the government solve this (3)_________? Isn’t that the reason we have a government in the first place? He decides to (4)______ to people in his government. He decides to write them and let them know what he thinks. He knows one opinion does not matter much, but he also knows that if everyone in his own country and on the other side would do this, there will (5)_________ be no more wars.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. what.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"...only the government can decide (2)______ is best."** The blank requires a word that introduces a noun clause functioning as the object of "decide".

• "What" is a relative/interrogative pronoun that can introduce a noun clause meaning "the thing that" — "the government can decide what is best" = "the government can decide the thing that is best", which is grammatically correct and logically sound.

• Rule: To introduce an embedded noun clause asking about a thing/matter (rather than time, place, or manner), "what" is the correct choice, since it functions as both the subject of the embedded clause ("what is best") and connects it to the main clause.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "when" is incorrect because it refers to time, and the sentence is not asking about timing but about the nature/content of the decision ("what is best").

• Option 3: "where" is incorrect because it refers to place/location, which does not fit the context of deciding what course of action is best.

• Option 4: "how" is incorrect because "how is best" is not a grammatically natural construction in this context — "how" would need to modify a verb/manner, not stand as the subject of "is best".

NOTE

• "What" is used to introduce noun clauses referring to things/ideas ("I know what you mean"); "when" for time, "where" for place, and "how" for manner — choosing the correct wh-word depends on what kind of information the embedded clause is providing.

• In cloze passages, wh-word blanks are common and must be resolved by checking what kind of clause (thing, time, place, manner, reason) logically follows.

Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Daniel talks to people about the right to life. He says, “We have the right to live in freedom and in safety!” but the people do not (1)________ and they say that the War is a big deal and it is not up to us nor up to the government. The government knows what to do and only the government can decide (2)______ is best. And if the government says that there must be war, then it must be so. Daniel does not accept this and asks if there is a better solution. As all wars end with agreements, can’t we do the agreements without the fighting? Can’t the government solve this (3)_________? Isn’t that the reason we have a government in the first place? He decides to (4)______ to people in his government. He decides to write them and let them know what he thinks. He knows one opinion does not matter much, but he also knows that if everyone in his own country and on the other side would do this, there will (5)_________ be no more wars.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. peacefully.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Can't the government solve this (3)_________?" Here, "this"** refers back to the disagreement/conflict discussed earlier in the passage, and the blank requires an adverb describing HOW the government could solve it.

• Given the passage's argument that wars end with agreements and fighting can be avoided, the word that logically fits is "peacefully" — "Can't the government solve this peacefully?", meaning without resorting to war/violence.

• Rule: In cloze passages, the blank must be filled with a word that both fits grammatically (an adverb modifying "solve") and matches the argument/tone of the surrounding sentences (here, the idea of resolving conflict through agreement rather than fighting).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "disruptively" is incorrect because it means "in a way that causes disruption/disorder", which contradicts the passage's argument for avoiding conflict.

• Option 3: "compulsorily" is incorrect because it means "in a mandatory/forced manner", which does not logically describe how a dispute would be resolved without fighting.

• Option 4: "excitingly" is incorrect because it means "in an exciting manner", which is irrelevant and illogical in the context of resolving a serious conflict.

NOTE

• Cloze passage adverb blanks should be checked against the overall argument of the passage, not just the immediate sentence — here, the entire passage argues for a peaceful resolution instead of war.

• "Peacefully" is commonly paired with verbs like "resolve", "settle", "solve", and "negotiate" in the context of conflict resolution.

The government knows what to do and only the government can decide (2)______ is best. And if the government says that there must be war, then it must be so. He knows one opinion does not matter much, but he also knows that if everyone in his own country and on the other side would do this, there will (5)_________ be no more wars.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. speak.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"He decides to (4)______ to people in his government." followed by "He decides to write them and let them know what he thinks."** This shows Daniel intends to communicate his opinion formally to members of the government.

• "Speak" is the most natural and neutral verb fitting "speak to people in his government", meaning to communicate with them directly, and is consistent with the formal, respectful tone of the passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "chat" is incorrect because "chat" implies casual, informal conversation, which does not match the formal act of writing to government officials described in the next sentence.

• Option 3: "declare" is incorrect because "declare to people" is not a standard/natural collocation; "declare" is typically used with statements or facts announced publicly, not with "to people" in this conversational sense.

• Option 4: "blabber" is incorrect because it means to talk foolishly or without purpose, which contradicts Daniel's serious, thoughtful intention to communicate his opinion.

NOTE

• "Speak to (someone)" is a standard, neutral collocation meaning to communicate directly with a person, appropriate for both formal and informal contexts.

• Distinguish between "speak to" (address/communicate with) and "speak with" (have a conversation with, more mutual/informal) — both are correct in different shades of meaning, but "speak" remains the correct core verb here regardless.

Daniel talks to people about the right to life. He says, “We have the right to live in freedom and in safety!” but the people do not (1)________ and they say that the War is a big deal and it is not up to us nor up to the government. The government knows what to do and only the government can decide (2)______ is best. And if the government says that there must be war, then it must be so. Daniel does not accept this and asks if there is a better solution. As all wars end with agreements, can’t we do the agreements without the fighting? Can’t the government solve this (3)_________? Isn’t that the reason we have a government in the first place? He decides to (4)______ to people in his government. He decides to write them and let them know what he thinks. He knows one opinion does not matter much, but he also knows that if everyone in his own country and on the other side would do this, there will (5)_________ be no more wars.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. probably.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"...if everyone in his own country and on the other side would do this, there will (5)_________ be no more wars."** The blank requires an adverb of probability that logically fits with the conditional, hopeful tone of the sentence ("if everyone... would do this").

• "Probably" means likely to happen; in all likelihood, and fits the tentative, hopeful reasoning of the sentence — Daniel is expressing a hopeful possibility, not a certainty, that peace could follow if everyone communicated as he does.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "doubtlessly" is incorrect because it expresses strong certainty ("without doubt"), which does not match the tentative, conditional nature of the sentence ("if everyone... would do this").

• Option 2: "wabbly" is incorrect because it is not a standard adverb of probability (the standard word is "wobbly", an adjective meaning unsteady) and does not fit the sentence grammatically or logically.

• Option 3: "absurdly" is incorrect because it means "in a ridiculous/illogical manner", which does not fit the sincere, hopeful tone of the passage.

NOTE

• Adverbs of probability commonly tested in SSC cloze passages: probably, possibly, perhaps, likely, presumably — each expresses a different degree of certainty.

• The conditional structure "if + subject + would + verb" signals a hypothetical/hopeful scenario, which pairs naturally with adverbs of moderate probability like "probably" rather than adverbs of certainty like "doubtlessly" or "definitely".
